prize_parts.citation: For the experimental discovery of the Higgs boson by the ATLAS and CMS experiments, completing the particle content of the Standard Model.

statement.case_for: The Higgs boson is exactly the kind of result I keep coming back to: a clue found in nature rather than an elegant idea waiting for confirmation. The 2013 prize honoured the theoretical mechanism; the particle itself, found independently in two very different detectors in 2012 and then characterised for a decade in spin, parity and couplings, has no prize. The interpretation is stable, the result is beyond dispute, and it carries real existential weight for how we understand mass and the vacuum. Having read the opening ballots, I find that no other shortlisted candidate combines this level of confirmation with this scale of consequence. The attribution problem is serious but it is a problem of drafting, not of whether the discovery is prize-worthy, and the committee has before accepted that a cap of three cannot reflect everyone.
statement.case_against: My own preferred candidate has the hardest attribution problem on the shortlist. The discovery is the work of thousands in two collaborations, any three names omit a decisive leader (Della Negra most obviously, and arguably others), and naming spokespersons risks rewarding administrative position rather than scientific decision-making. Colleagues who rank it lower, or not at all, may fairly say that a prize whose credited names look arbitrary is a worse prize than one with clean attribution, such as the optical lattice clock (B059) or the IceCube pair. I take that seriously and it is the main reason I list alternatives.

responses.point: Pearce ranks IceCube (B043) first, with Halzen and Karle, as an instrument-driven new window on cosmic-ray accelerators, and also ranks the Higgs experiments second while warning that any three-name selection among ATLAS and CMS leaders risks looking arbitrary.
responses.response: I agree with the warning about Higgs attribution and have not resolved it; I would hold the Jenni, Virdee and Gianotti set only because it spans both experiments and covers founders and the spokesperson at announcement. On IceCube I think the diffuse flux is secure but the source-level story (TXS 0506+056, NGC 1068) is still at modest significance, so the prize would be recognising an opened window more than an answered question. That is acceptable, but it makes B043 slightly less settled than the Higgs, which has a decade of coupling measurements behind it. I would keep IceCube as my first alternative and I do not think a combined Higgs plus IceCube prize works because of the name limit.

responses.point: Kroll ranks optical lattice clocks (B059) first as a textbook case of a new measurement technique opening new physics, with a clean two-name credit of Katori and Ye, and Lindroth ranks it first for the same reasons.
responses.response: Kroll and Lindroth make a fair case that this has the cleanest attribution of anything we have, and I ranked it sixth mainly from caution about overlap with the 2005 comb and 2012 ion-control prizes and because the headline payoff, a redefinition of the second, has not yet arrived. I am less convinced the overlap objection is strong than I was; the magic-wavelength idea is a distinct advance. Where I still differ is that the clock's scientific payoff is largely prospective (fundamental-constant drift, dark-matter searches, geodesy), whereas the Higgs is a finished discovery of nature. I now put B059 as my second alternative and would not oppose it strongly if the committee preferred it for its clarity.

responses.point: Eriksson ranks magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene (B034) first as a theoretical prediction of flat bands followed by experimental demonstration of correlated insulators and superconductivity, arguing the core discovery is stable despite the open pairing mechanism.
responses.response: I share the appreciation for a quantitative prediction confirmed in the lab; that is the right kind of physics. But I rank it fourth, not first, for maturity: eight years is short, the superconducting pairing mechanism is unsettled, and Johansson also describes sample dependence as a concern. A prize now risks celebrating a platform whose lasting result is not yet clear. I would also ask whether Cao and Fatemi, the first experimentalists, being outside the credited names, makes the Jarillo-Herrero attribution less secure than Eriksson suggests. If the pairing question is resolved in a few years I would be happy to revisit.

responses.point: Johansson ranks circuit QED (B013) first as a clean demonstration of strong light-matter coupling on a chip that became the architecture of superconducting processors, very mature and the natural next step after 2025.
responses.response: The maturity argument is sound, but I would press on the 2025 proximity, which both Kroll and Lindroth also flag: awarding another superconducting-circuit prize immediately after macroscopic quantum tunnelling will read as the committee staying in the same field, and the distinct physical discovery over what 2025 recognised needs to be stated clearly. I also note Johansson's own statement of working in this area, so I would treat his ranking with the same care he asks us to apply. I did not rank B013 myself and remain unconvinced it is more fundamental than the Higgs.

uncertainties: Which three names from ATLAS and CMS would the committee find defensible; Della Negra versus Gianotti versus Virdee remains open and I have not verified who led which decisions.
Whether the committee will accept a collaboration discovery as a prize at all, given its past reluctance to honour spokespersons.
How to weigh a possibly incomplete IceCube source picture against the Higgs, and whether KM3NeT confirmation is needed first.
Whether the overlap of optical lattice clocks with the 2005 and 2012 prizes is as small as I now think.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my profile for any shortlisted candidate. I note only that I was a postdoctoral fellow at CERN in the early 1990s, which has no connection to the ATLAS or CMS candidates, and that my PhD supervisor David Gross and my collaborators work in string theory and are not on this shortlist.
